notes.meaning: Under the first covenant, God gave his people specific rules for worship and an earthly sacred tent called the tabernacle. A covenant is a solemn binding agreement made between God and his people. Because this sanctuary was built by human hands out of worldly materials, it was temporary and served as an earthly copy of heavenly realities.

The front room of this sacred tent was called the Holy Place. Inside stood a golden lampstand that supplied light where there were no windows, along with a table holding twelve loaves of holy bread. These loaves showed God's daily care and fellowship with the twelve tribes of Israel.

Behind a heavy inner curtain was the Most Holy Place, which held the golden altar of incense and the gold-covered chest called the ark of the covenant. Inside the chest were a jar of manna, Aaron's blossoming rod, and the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments. Above it were winged figures called cherubim whose wings covered the mercy seat, the golden lid where God showed mercy when sacrificial blood was sprinkled.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars translate the golden censer as the incense altar, explaining that while the altar stood physically outside the curtain, it belonged functionally to the Most Holy Place because its incense was used there.

notes.meaning: Ordinary priests entered the outer room every day to care for the lamps and offer incense. The inner room was far more restricted, since only the high priest could enter it once a year on the Day of Atonement. He never went in without animal blood to offer for his own sins and for the sins the people committed in ignorance.

The Holy Spirit used this arrangement to teach an important lesson. As long as the earthly tabernacle and its ritual system remained in place, the true path into God's heavenly presence was not yet revealed. The closed room showed that ordinary sinners were still kept at a distance from God.

The tabernacle served as a living picture for that era, showing that animal gifts and sacrifices could never fully clear guilt from the worshipper's inner conscience. Its rules dealt mainly with outward things like foods, drinks, and ceremonial washings. God imposed these external duties only until the time of reformation, when Christ would arrive to set everything right.

Christ came as the High Priest of the real spiritual blessings that have now arrived. He did not minister in an earthly tent, but entered the greater and perfect sanctuary in heaven. He did not bring the blood of goats and calves, but entered God's presence once for all by his own blood, securing eternal redemption, which is full rescue from the penalty of sin.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching holds that Christ continually presents his once-for-all offering to the Father in heaven, and that this same sacrifice is made present upon the altar during the Mass.

notes.meaning: Under the law of Moses, sprinkling animal blood or the ashes of a young cow could restore ceremonial purity to an unclean body. Christ's sacrifice accomplishes something infinitely greater. Because he offered himself without any moral blemish through the eternal Spirit, his blood cleanses our inner consciences from dead works, freeing us to serve the living God with pure hearts.

Christ is the mediator, or go-between, of a new covenant so that God's chosen people can receive the promised eternal inheritance. His death on the cross paid the full penalty for sins committed under the first covenant, which animal blood could never wipe away. This one sacrifice gives believers true and lasting peace with God.

In ordinary life, a last will and testament only takes effect after the person who wrote it has died. No one can claim an inheritance while the person who promised it is still alive. In the same way, the blessings of God's covenant were formally released to believers through the death of Christ.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars argue the passage refers to a covenant rather than a will, translating the term as an appointed sacrificial victim that had to be slain over dead animals to confirm the agreement.

notes.meaning: This explains why even the first covenant under Moses was put into effect with blood. God showed from the very start that sinful people cannot enter into a covenant relationship with him without a life being given. Blood proved that the agreement was sacred, serious, and binding.

After Moses read all the commandments of the law to the assembly, he took animal blood mixed with water and sprinkled both the scroll and the people using scarlet wool and hyssop branches. As he did this, he announced that the blood confirmed the covenant God had commanded them to keep. This solemn ceremony bound God and his people together in fellowship.

Moses also sprinkled blood over the tabernacle and every bowl and tool used in priestly worship. Under the Old Testament law, nearly everything had to be purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there was no forgiveness of sins. This pointed forward to the cross, showing that God never overlooks sin without an atoning sacrifice.

The earthly tent and its utensils were copies of realities in heaven, so animal blood was sufficient to consecrate them for worship. But the true heavenly sanctuary required a far superior sacrifice. Christ's own blood was needed to open the way so that redeemed sinners could enter God's holy presence.

Christ did not enter a physical sanctuary built by human hands, which was only an earthly sketch of the real one. Instead, he ascended directly into heaven to appear before God the Father on our behalf. There he continuously stands as our heavenly High Priest, pleading the merits of his sacrifice for our rescue.

The Levitical high priest had to enter the Most Holy Place year after year with animal blood, but Christ does not need to offer himself repeatedly. If his sacrifice were like the old ones, he would have had to suffer and die over and over throughout human history. Instead, he appeared once for all at the climax of the ages to wipe away sin by offering himself.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching explains that the Mass does not repeat the suffering or death of Christ, but re-presents his one finished sacrifice in an unbloody manner, applying its graces to the faithful.

notes.meaning: Every person is appointed by God to die once, and after death comes judgment. There are no second chances or repeated lifetimes to make things right with God. Because earthly life happens only once, each person's eternal future is decided before death arrives.

Just as human beings die only once, Christ was offered once on the cross to carry the punishment for the sins of many. When he returns a second time, he will not come to bear sin or die as an offering again. He will come in glory to deliver full and final salvation to everyone who eagerly waits for him.
